In the year 1500, the world took a dramatic turn, one that would forever alter the course of human history. The Black Death, which had ravaged Europe in the 14th century, had a profound impact on the social and economic structures of the time. As the plague receded, the feudal system, which had been on the brink of collapse, began to reassert itself.

    The nobility, who had long held power and influence, saw an opportunity to reassert their dominance. They began to consolidate their power, using the weakened state of the common people to their advantage. The peasants, who had been the backbone of the feudal system, were forced to accept even more stringent conditions, including higher taxes and increased labor requirements.

    As the years passed, the feudal system continued to evolve, with the nobility becoming increasingly powerful and the common people becoming more and more marginalized. The concept of a unified, centralized government gave way to a patchwork of local lordships and fiefdoms, each with its own unique system of governance.

    In this world, the concept of a "middle class" never really developed. The nobility and clergy held all the power, while the common people were relegated to the lower rungs of society. The idea of social mobility was all but impossible, as birth and station determined one's place in the world.

    Despite the hardships and injustices, the feudal system continued to thrive. The nobility invested heavily in the arts and culture, commissioning grand works of architecture, literature, and music. The universities of Europe became centers of learning, attracting scholars and intellectuals from across the continent.

    As the centuries passed, the feudal system continued to evolve, with new technologies and innovations emerging to support its structures. The invention of the printing press, for example, allowed the nobility to disseminate their propaganda and ideology more widely, further solidifying their grip on power.

    In this world, the concept of a "revolution" never really occurred. The nobility were too powerful, and the common people too entrenched in their ways, to ever challenge the status quo. The idea of a "democracy" was seen as a threat to the established order, and was therefore never seriously considered.

    As the world entered the modern era, the feudal system continued to dominate. The Industrial Revolution, which had transformed the world in our timeline, never occurred. Instead, the nobility continued to rely on manual labor and traditional crafts to sustain their economies.

    In this world, the concept of a "global economy" never really developed. Trade was limited to the nobility and the wealthy, who controlled the flow of goods and services across the continent. The idea of a "world market" was seen as a threat to the established order, and was therefore never seriously considered.

    As the centuries passed, the feudal system continued to evolve, with new technologies and innovations emerging to support its structures. The world was a vastly different place, one in which the nobility held all the power, and the common people were relegated to the lower rungs of society.

    In this world, the concept of a "utopia" was seen as a myth, a fantasy created by the idealistic and the naive. The feudal system was the only system that had ever truly existed, and it would continue to dominate the world for centuries to come.

    And so, the world continued on its path, a world of lords and vassals, of nobles and commoners. A world in which the concept of social justice was seen as a threat to the established order, and was therefore never seriously considered.

    The feudal system had become the norm, and it would continue to shape the world for centuries to come.
